detail.title: Architectural Form Generation Driven by Text-Guided Generative Modeling Based on Intent Image Reconstruction and Multi-Criteria Evaluation
detail.abstract: This study presents an integrated workflow for early-stage architectural form generation by combining text-guided generative models with parametric modeling tools. The process transforms natural language cues into editable 3D geometric models. Conceptual images are generated using diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion and Midjourney under semantic control. These images are processed through contour extraction and scale mapping to reconstruct approximate volume models in Rhino-Grasshopper. Geometric constraints and scale rules ensure consistency across scenarios. For evaluation, a multi-criteria framework-including volume, openness, and symmetry-is applied to support transparent scheme selection. Visualization tools like radar charts and comparison matrices assist in design analysis and optimization. A case study of an airport terminal demonstrates the workflow' s effectiveness: 64 variants were generated with 4.2 times more diversity than manual concepts. The process also revealed improved area-to-volume and surface-to-height ratios. The results highlight the semantic control enabled by text-guided generation and the value of parametric platforms for early geometric evaluation.

title: A Conceptual Study on Reducing Workplace Bias and Enhancing Productivity through Inclusive Decision-Making Processes
affiliations: PSGR Krishnammal College for Women and PSGR Krishnammal College for Women

detail.title: A Conceptual Study on Reducing Workplace Bias and Enhancing Productivity through Inclusive Decision-Making Processes
detail.abstract: Bias in workplace decision-making remains a significant barrier in creating equitable and highperforming organizations. These biases, whether implicit or explicit, can negatively impact employee morale, limit access to diverse perspectives, and hinder innovation. Consequently, organizations experiencing unchecked workplace bias often face challenges such as reduced employee engagement, higher turnover rates, and inefficiencies in decision-making processes, all of which affect productivity. This paper explores the transformative potential of inclusive decision-making as a tool to address workplace bias and enhance organizational productivity. Inclusive decision-making emphasizes the equitable representation of diverse voices, transparent processes, and psychological safety, fostering an environment where employees can fully engage and contribute. Through a conceptual framework, the paper links inclusivity practices with productivity outcomes, identifying critical strategies such as unconscious bias training, diverse team representation, and feedback mechanisms. This paper also highlights areas for future research, including longitudinal studies on inclusivity's impact, cross-cultural variations in inclusive practices, and the role of technology in enabling bias-free decision-making. By addressing workplace bias and prioritizing inclusivity, organizations can enhance their effectiveness and align with broader goals of equity and social responsibility.

detail.abstract: Team emergent states (TES) represent dynamic properties of teams that are cognitive, affective, and motivational states of teams, and which vary as function of team context, inputs, processes, and outcomes. TES constructs have a theoretical origin residing at lower levels of analysis (i.e., individual) that arise over time to characterize the team as a whole. TES are key variables in team effectiveness models. These are distinct from team processes, which refer to the actions team members take to combine their individual resources, knowledge, and skills to achieve collective goals. Until the early 2000s, TES were often erroneously considered team processes. Since being clearly distinguished from team processes, the nature of TES has gained conceptual clarity, and the TES literature has evolved considerably. TES are typically conceptualized as playing a mediating role in input-mediator-outcome (IMO) models of team effectiveness, which depict inputs (I) as antecedent factors (e.g., team composition, design, leadership) that influence mediating mechanisms (M) such as team processes and team emergent states, which subsequently impact team outcomes (O) such as team performance. However, TES are also frequently examined as predictor, moderator, and outcome factors in studies today. There are numerous specific types of TES that can be classified into different categories depending upon whether the focal construct is cognitive, affective, or motivational in nature. The fundamental conclusion of this body of research is that a variety of factors can encourage the development of team emergent states, which have important implications for team processes and other team emergent states as well as team-level and, sometimes, individual-level effectiveness outcomes.

title: The Codex of Authority
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: The Codex of Authority
detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of the Codex of Authority, a juridical metaphor for the compiled rule that governs without reference to a legislator. In predictive societies, authority is no longer produced by political will but by syntactic form. From automated drafts of the EU’s AI Act to blockchain smart contracts, institutional norms emerge as self-sufficient codices where legitimacy resides in structure rather than origin. By analyzing this shift, the article proposes a framework for understanding how legal authority becomes executable, impersonal, and detached from interpretation.

title: Too Many Teams? Examining The Impact of Multiple Team Memberships and Permanent Team Identification on Employees’ Identity Strain, Cognitive Depletion, and Turnover

detail.abstract: As the prevalence of multiple team membership (MTM) arrangements continues to grow, researchers have argued that shifting between teams and work roles induces MTM identity strain and other harmful outcomes. Drawing from work role transitions research on role identity and integrating it with social identity theory, we investigate this line of reasoning by conducting two studies, one field and one online panel study, focusing on blended MTMs, in which employees are concurrently assigned to a permanent team and several temporary project teams. Specifically, we examine the theoretical mechanisms explaining a positive relationship between number of temporary teams and turnover decisions. In Study 1, we surprisingly found that number of temporary teams negatively related to turnover decisions through MTM identity strain with permanent team identification strengthening this effect. In contrast, in Study 2, we found support for the hypothesized relationships: number of teams indirectly positively related to turnover intentions, mediated by MTM identity strain and cognitive depletion, and permanent team identification weakened the indirect effect. We provide explanations for these mixed findings and suggest theoretical and practical implications for MTM research.

title: Functional Fitness: Improving Retention and Fighting "Brain Drain"
affiliations: Duke University, Department of Political Science, Students and George Mason University

detail.title: Functional Fitness: Improving Retention and Fighting "Brain Drain"

publicationDetails.detailsText: US Army War College's War Room Journal, 28 AUG 2025 (online)

detail.abstract: The U.S. Army faces significant officer retention challenges, with only 47% of company-grade officers continuing service beyond their initial obligation. Critics argue that functional area specializations either create "brain drain" by attracting top combat arms performers or serve as refuges for underperforming officers. This study empirically tests both assertions using RAND data (2012-2019) and pilot survey evidence. Results contradict the brain drain hypothesis: functional areas do not universally attract top performers from basic branches. However, officers transitioning to functional areas demonstrate improved promotion rates, suggesting better talent-position alignment. Survey data reveals 62% of functional area officers would have left military service entirely without transfer opportunities, rising to 69% under the Blended Retirement System. Findings demonstrate that functional areas serve as critical retention mechanisms preserving institutional knowledge while addressing officers' needs for career autonomy and meaningful work. Rather than depleting combat arms talent, functional areas prevent civilian exodus, representing strategic talent investments

publicationDetails.detailsText: Proceedings of the 9th CIPM International Research Symposium – Sri Lanka 2025

detail.abstract: Despite the passage of many years, organizations remain focused on retaining their workforce. However, a significant challenge has emerged in Sri Lanka, where nursing officers are increasingly less likely to continue working in hospitals. This trend poses a critical issue for the country's healthcare industry. In response, this study aims to evaluate how satisfaction with the organizational climate influences the retention of nursing officers in base hospitals within the Ampara District. The study focused on nursing officers working in base hospitals in the Ampara District, Sri Lanka. Data was collected using a self-administered questionnaire distributed to 142 nursing officers, of which 128 were returned fully completed. The findings revealed a strong positive correlation (r = 0.713) between satisfaction with the organizational climate and employee retention. Simple regression analysis results showed an R-square value of 0.508 and an adjusted R value of 0.501, indicating that approximately 50% of the variation in employee retention among nursing officers can be attributed to their satisfaction with the organizational climate. Furthermore, the unstandardized beta value for satisfaction with organizational climate (SOC) was 0.677, suggesting that a one-unit increase in SOC results in a 0.677-unit increase in employee retention (ER).

The present study examined the effectiveness of hybrid workplace culture among IT employees working in various organizations in Chennai. The main research questions in this study concern the multi-gen workforce and employee engagement in a hybrid workplace environment and the study aimed to analyze whether the hybrid workplace culture promotes trust, flexibility, support, communication and productivity among the multi-gen employees. The study concluded that multi-gen employees have to come forward in organizations to work together, collaborate and gain from engagement with one another.

title: Perceiving AI in the Newsroom: Gender, Experience, and Framing Effects Among Iranian Journalists

detail.title: Perceiving AI in the Newsroom: Gender, Experience, and Framing Effects Among Iranian Journalists
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of AI across diverse sectors has prompted profound transformations in professional practices, including journalism. This study investigates how Iranian journalists perceive and evaluate AI within their professional environment, focusing on the ways narrative framing shapes attitudes toward its adoption. Using an Experimental Vignette Survey (EVS) design, 143 journalists (91 men, 52 women) were randomly assigned to one of three vignette conditions presenting AI as a productivity tool, a threat to professional autonomy, or a neutral technology. Participants completed a structured questionnaire assessing perceived usefulness, trust in AI-generated content, ethical concerns, and job security anxiety. Descriptive analyses revealed generally moderate optimism about AI's utility alongside high levels of ethical apprehension and concern over job security. Manipulation checks confirmed that framing significantly influenced cognitive and emotional responses: positive framings enhanced perceptions of usefulness, while threatoriented framings amplified skepticism and anxiety. Regression and subgroup analyses indicated that gender and professional experience moderated these effects, with women showing greater sensitivity to framing and experienced journalists reporting lower levels of job threat. These findings highlight the importance of narrative context in shaping professional attitudes toward emerging technologies and underscore the need for culturally specific research on AI in journalism.

detail.title: Impact of GST and Issues Faced by Hotel Industry
detail.abstract: This research article examines the complex dynamics surrounding the implementation of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in the hotel industry. Through a combination of quantitative data and qualitative insights, the study highlights the transformative impact of GST on financial transparency, tax evasion reduction, and a more efficient tax filing system, while also addressing the challenges faced by hotels due to the intricate tax framework, emphasizing the importance of effective communication and targeted training. The article concludes by advocating for collaboration between the hotel sector and policymakers to refine the GST framework, enabling the industry to capitalize on positive changes and navigate challenges for sustained growth in an ever-evolving economic context.

title: How Do Ceos Seek Advice from CMOs Vs. CTOs in Radical Innovation Decision Making?
affiliations: Macquarie University, Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School, Jonkoping University - Jonkoping International Business School (JIBS), Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School and Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: How Do Ceos Seek Advice from CMOs Vs. CTOs in Radical Innovation Decision Making?
detail.abstract: In situations of high uncertainty, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) advice seeking is of critical importance to access additional knowledge to inform their strategic decisions, such as in relation to radical innovation. Yet, little research has investigated the underlying mechanisms of CEO advice seeking in radical innovation decisions-especially when CEOs face conflicting advice. Using data from two discrete choice experiments (249 CEOs and 155 CEOs, respectively), complemented by ten qualitative interviews with CEOs, Chief Marketing Officers (CMOs) and Chief Technology Officers (CTOs), we investigate how conflicting advice from CMOs and CTOs affects CEO choices in radical innovation projects, contingent on various degrees of market and technological uncertainty. Subsequently, by using additional survey data (166 CEOs), we assess how external advice seeking affects the relationship between advice seeking from CTOs and CMOs and firms' radical innovation performance under market and technological uncertainty. Given conflicting CMO vs. CTO advice, our results indicate that when a radical innovation project is characterized by high technological uncertainty, CEOs are more likely to choose radical innovation projects that the CTO supports, even if the CMO does not. Yet, surprisingly, we do not find that CEOs' radical innovation decisions are affected by CMOs' supporting advice when an innovation project faces high market uncertainty. Finally, we find that the positive effect of CEO advice seeking from CMOs (CTOs) on firms' radical innovation performance is strengthened if the CEO also seeks external advice under high market (technological) uncertainty.

title: Time Toxicity in CBCT-Guided Radiation Therapy: A Retrospective Analysis of Unplanned Imaging Burden Across Disease Sites

detail.title: Time Toxicity in CBCT-Guided Radiation Therapy: A Retrospective Analysis of Unplanned Imaging Burden Across Disease Sites
detail.abstract: PurposeAdaptive radiotherapy (ART) enhances treatment precision by adjusting for anatomical changes identified during a course of treatment. While ART is resource-intensive, non-adaptive workflows may also incur significant time and resource burden due to reactive interventions. This study aims to quantify the time-related burden of unplanned activities in non-adaptive CBCT-guided radiation therapy and assess their impact on patients, caregivers, and departmental efficiency.Methods and MaterialsA retrospective analysis was conducted on 300 patients treated with CBCT-guided radiation therapy across 20 treatment techniques, encompassing 6,887 treatment fractions. Unplanned activities—including repeated CBCT acquisitions, aborted treatment sessions, additional CT scans, and mid-course replanning—were identified through electronic medical records and imaging logs. Time burden was estimated using electronic medical record timestamps.ResultsRepeated CBCTs occurred in 55% of patients, contributing to 201.9 hours of additional imaging time. Pelvic disease sites, particularly bladder and gynecologic cancers, exhibited the highest frequency of repeat imaging. Six patients required rescheduling due to unresolved anatomical discrepancies, and 15 underwent treatment plan modifications, with nine requiring repeat planning CTs. The average additional time per affected fraction was 13 minutes (range: 2–219 minutes), with some sessions extending beyond 3 hours.ConclusionsNon-adaptive CBCT-guided workflows can lead to substantial time toxicity, comparable to or exceeding the resource demands of ART. These findings underscore the need for improved documentation, selective ART implementation, and workflow optimization to enhance patient experience and institutional efficiency.

detail.abstract: A team charter is a formal document written by team members at the outset of a team’s life cycle that outlines a team’s purpose, goals, team member roles and, responsibilities, as well as plans related to how team members will work together. This, article begins by defining team charters and outlining the various reasons that they are, beneficial to teams, their interactions, and performance. The article also advances practical, research-backed recommendations about the development of team charters, addressing issues including when teams should create team charters, who should be involved in creating team charters, what should be included in team charters, and, when team charters should be revised. In summary, the article offers evidence-based, recommendations that may be useful to team members, team leaders, and managers, interested in leveraging the power of team charters in an effort to get teams off to a good start and perform effectively over time.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Structured Path Resonance Loop (SPRL), a collaborative language protocol designed for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). While models such as GPT-5, Claude 3, and Gemini 1.5 demonstrate strong reasoning and orchestration capabilities, their interfaces remain tied to linear prompts, limiting multi-turn memory, role coordination, and structural control. SPRL provides a tag-based protocol layer—including @path, @module, @beat, @resonance, @handover, and @pause/A⁻¹—that makes reasoning paths, rhythm, and role handovers explicit and navigable. We propose a five-layer interface model situating SPRL between cognitive planning and language generation, enabling reproducible, auditable, and reversible collaboration. Deployment options include lightweight tagging within prompts, parser-mediated middleware, and deep integration with tool/plugin ecosystems. Application scenarios range from legal drafting and educational writing to software co-generation and clinical summarization. SPRL reframes language not as a semantic request but as an operable collaboration interface, offering a foundation for open standards in structured reasoning and multi-agent coordination.

detail.title: Study on Exploring the Optimization Path of Financial Supply Chain and the Improvement of Enterprise Economic Benefits by Integrating Graph Neural Networks Driven by Big Data
detail.abstract: To optimize financial supply chain processes and enhance enterprise economic benefits, it is necessary to fully integrate big data-driven technical means to mine key correlation information in the supply chain. Practice shows that integrating knowledge graphs as a core auxiliary tool into financial supply chain analysis can effectively identify value nodes and risk points in the supply chain by deeply mining the correlation attributes among various participants, capital flows, logistics, and other entities in the supply chain, thereby providing accurate support for the optimization of resource allocation. Inspired by the technical ideas of Graph Attention Neural Networks (GAT) and KGCN (Knowledge Graph Convolutional Network), this study designs an attention embedding propagation layer to aggregate the neighbor feature information of financial supply chain entities in the knowledge graph, thereby enriching the feature representation of various elements in the supply chain. Experimental results on three real financial supply chain datasets show that this method achieves the best performance in scenarios such as SME financing matching and supply chain capital flow optimization, and also achieves significant results in cross-enterprise credit evaluation scenarios, providing a practical technical path for improving enterprise economic benefits.

detail.abstract: A restructuring of Venezuela’s and Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A ’s debt remains an elusive prospect. However, for Venezuela to revitalize its oil and gas sector, Venezuela and Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. (“Pdvsa”) need to re-connect with the international financial community, oil majors, international oil services providers, investors and customers. To re-connect and be able to develop their main hard currency revenue source, Venezuela and Pdvsa need to restructure their debt or at least start to seriously engage with the international financial community, including the official sector, for multiple reasons: (i) Legal Exposure of Pdvsa’s Exports. Pdvsa’s exports, and more specifically PDVSA Petróleo, S.A.’s1 exports2 are exposed to attachments and other remedies ─provisional or in aid of execution of judgments─ sought or already rendered in favor of their myriad creditors. For example, crude shipments that belong to PDVSA Petróleo, S.A. (“Ppsa”) while en route to customers, are exposed to this risk. (ii) Risk to Financial Transactions. Loan proceeds disbursed into accounts that belong to Pdvsa or certain affiliates, pre-payments for crude oil made by customers and deposited into Pdvsa’s accounts may also be exposed to this attachment risk3 . (iii) Broad Exposure of Hard Currency Revenues. Virtually any other hard currency payments and even crypto currencies received outside Venezuela by Venezuela, Pdvsa or its affiliates (such as payments for dividends, interest, insurance indemnities, rebates, compensation for damages, purchase price adjustments on oil shipments, among many other) are all exposed to the risk of creditors seizing, attaching or otherwise taking control of those funds to satisfy judgments, arbitration awards, trade and commercial debt and financial indebtedness.

title: Privacy-Aware Sequential Learning
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh and University of Pitttsburgh

detail.title: Privacy-Aware Sequential Learning
detail.abstract: In settings like vaccination registries, individuals act after observing others, and the resulting public records can expose private information. We study privacy-preserving sequential learning, where agents add endogenous noise to their reported actions to conceal private signals. Efficient social learning relies on information flow, seemingly in conflict with privacy. Surprisingly, with continuous signals and a fixed privacy budget $(\varepsilon)$, the optimal randomization strategy balances privacy and accuracy, accelerating learning to $\Theta_{\varepsilon}(\log n)$, faster than the nonprivate $\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$ rate. In the nonprivate baseline, the expected time to the first correct action and the number of incorrect actions diverge; under privacy with sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, both are finite. Privacy helps because, under the false state, agents more often receive signals contradicting the majority; randomization then asymmetrically amplifies the log-likelihood ratio, enhancing aggregation. In heterogeneous populations, an order-optimal $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$ rate is achievable when a subset of agents have low privacy budgets. With binary signals, however, privacy reduces informativeness and impairs learning relative to the nonprivate baseline, though the dependence on $\varepsilon$ is nonmonotone. Our results show how privacy reshapes information dynamics and inform the design of platforms and policies.

detail.abstract: This study examines the implications of the EU Deforestation-Free Products Regulation (EU-2023/1115), a 2023 statute governing trade in deforestation-linked commodities such as tea, coffee, spices, rubber, and timber. The regulation’s stringent due diligence and traceability norms pose significant challenges and open new opportunities for India’s agricultural exports. The study proposes a comprehensive digital governance model across all supply chain stages to ensure regulatory conformity, enhance traceability, and promote sustainable exports aligned with global environmental and sustainability benchmarks.

title: Personalized Pricing Through Strategic User Profiling in Social Networks
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Singapore University of Technology and Design and Chinese University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Personalized Pricing Through Strategic User Profiling in Social Networks

publicationDetails.detailsText: IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, volume 32, issue 5, 2024[10.1109/TNET.2024.3410976]

detail.abstract: Traditional user profiling techniques rely on browsing history or purchase records to identify users' willingness to pay. This enables sellers to offer personalized prices to profiled users while charging only a uniform price to non-profiled users. However, the emergence of privacy-enhancing technologies has caused users to actively avoid on-site data tracking. Today, major online sellers have turned to public platforms such as online social networks to better track users' profiles from their product-related discussions. This paper presents the first analytical study on how users should best manage their social activities against potential personalized pricing, and how a seller should strategically adjust her pricing scheme to facilitate user profiling in social networks. We formulate a dynamic Bayesian game played between the seller and users under asymmetric information. The key challenge of analyzing this game comes from the double couplings between the seller and the users as well as among the users. Furthermore, the equilibrium analysis needs to ensure consistency between users' revealed information and the seller's belief under random user profiling. We address these challenges by alternately applying backward and forward induction, and successfully characterize the unique perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) in closed form. Our analysis reveals that as the accuracy of profiling technology improves, the seller tends to raise the equilibrium uniform price to motivate users' increased social activities and facilitate user profiling. However, this results in most users being worse off after the informed consent policy is imposed to ensure users' awareness of data access and profiling practices by potential sellers. This finding suggests that recent regulatory evolution towards enhancing users' privacy awareness may have unintended consequences of reducing users' payoffs. Finally, we examine prevalent pricing practices where the seller breaks a pricing promise to personalize final offerings, and show that it only slightly improves the seller's average revenue while introducing higher variance.

title: Invoicing Currency and Optimal Policies in a Global Liquidity Trap
affiliations: Yonsei University, Yonsei University, School of Economics, Yonsei University and New York University

detail.title: Invoicing Currency and Optimal Policies in a Global Liquidity Trap
detail.abstract: We study how international pricing regimes shape optimal monetary-fiscal policy mix during global liquidity trap episodes. Using a two-country New Keynesian model under alternative pricing assumptions, we find that when exchange rate pass-through is high, the less affected economy optimally raises interest rates to manage relative prices between countries, though at the cost of suppressing global demand. However, when pass-through is limited, it maintains low rates to support global demand instead. This monetary policy divergence widens with shock severity, reflecting that high pass-through makes exchange rate management a more effective tool for stabilizing relative prices, though at the cost of suppressing global demand. Fiscal policy complements monetary policy by addressing its limitations: under high pass-through, it focuses on expanding government spending across both countries to boost suppressed global demand, while under low pass-through, it implements asymmetric spending increases concentrated in the more affected country to correct relative imbalances. When there is dominant currency pricing, counterparty policy rates generally fall between high and low pass-through cases, but vary significantly with the shock's origin due to asymmetric trade channels and monetary policy transmission.

detail.abstract: The stability of Northeast Asia, particularly the Korean Peninsula, is crucial for global security and economic growth. The region remains highly contentious due to the competing interests of the United States, China, Russia, Japan, and South Korea, with North Korea's nuclear capabilities posing a significant threat to peace. Addressing these challenges is vital as the increasing tensions and shifting great power dynamics could lead to destabilization and conflict. Economic interdependence among Japan, South Korea, and China is substantial, yet historical grievances often inhibit security collaboration. The power dynamics in the region have evolved from a post-World War II bipolarity into a complex interplay marked by the influences of China and Russia, affecting responses to North Korea. Moreover, efforts to resolve the North Korean crisis through comprehensive agreements have stalled; instead, a focus on manageable, incremental engagements is necessary for fostering trust and stability. Failure to address these emerging challenges risks further entrenching historical animosities and fostering instability, which in turn could jeopardize economic relationships and security alliances. The absence of effective diplomacy may lead to increased militarization, potential conflict escalation, and disrupted trade flows, with significant consequences for regional and global security frameworks. To foster stability in the region, it is recommended to establish a Northeast Asia Stabilization Forum to facilitate ongoing dialogue and manage security issues collaboratively. Strengthening economic integration initiatives through mutual benefit-focused joint ventures among Japan, South Korea, and China is also vital. Additionally, coordinating humanitarian and development projects can enhance goodwill and compliance with broader security measures. A shift towards incremental diplomatic strategies that prioritize phased confidence-building measures with North Korea is essential. Engaging external actors such as the U.S. and the European Union will support regional stability through shared economic and security initiatives. In conclusion, creating a stable regional order in Northeast Asia is imperative not just for immediate crisis management but also for securing long-term peace and prosperity. By implementing these recommendations, regional actors can work towards a cooperative future that prioritizes security and economic growth, positioning Northeast Asia as a fundamental pillar of a peaceful global order.

title: Coal Mine Closure from a Lens Restorative Justice, Human Rights, and Corporate Due Diligence for a Just Transition in Colombia

detail.title: Coal Mine Closure from a Lens Restorative Justice, Human Rights, and Corporate Due Diligence for a Just Transition in Colombia

declarations.funderStatement: This research was sponsored through the Colfuturo Scholarship.

detail.abstract:
A just energy transition is a central topic in discussions about the future of energy, mainly since the commitment of 196 countries in the 2015 Paris Agreement to prevent global temperatures from rising 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Efforts are concentrated on limiting the increase to approximately 1.5 degrees to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. 

Colombia has set ambitious short-term greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction targets (51% by 2030) and a long-term goal of carbon neutrality by 2050. Achieving these objectives necessitates a profound transformation driven by the Energy Transition Policy. The policy mandates a shift from less than 1% to over 12% in the energy matrix by 2022 for non-conventional renewable energies, a GHG emissions reduction target from 20% to 51% by 2030, and the prioritisation of ‘sustainable recovery’ as the cornerstone of the economic recovery strategy post-COVID 19.

However, as the sixth-largest global coal exporter, Colombia faces an uncertain future. The geopolitical aftermath of the Ukrainian war has underscored the imperative to ensure energy security and expedite the transition to renewable energy sources. While an immediate economic opportunity exists for Colombia, the long-term outlook involves an escalating decline in coal demand. Climate policies and the rapid growth of renewables, with an expected global drop in coal demand through 2030, increasingly pressure coal's role in the power sector.

The current Colombian energy transition policy, acknowledging the need for decarbonisation, does not envision provisions for repairing human rights impacts during the dismantling of coal operations. The existing legal frameworks on mine closure do not also consider human rights issues to remedy the adverse impacts caused to the affected communities during closure and post-closure. Questions arise regarding the Colombian government's ability to adapt and respond to the real-time decline in coal demand and potential closure operations. The consequences of the lack of preparation for these scenarios extend beyond the environment and the economy and land on the human rights of the individuals and dependent communities in the sector, such as La Guajira and Cesar departments.
This scenario calls for a fair and equitable framework for the energy transition in the coal sector, prioritising the human rights of nature, individuals and populations dependent on the industry. Specific regulation focusing on human rights is required to establish clear obligations for authorities and companies during mine closure and post-closure of coal operations. The principles of restorative justice and the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights provide a robust framework for states and companies to identify harm, assign responsibility, repair damage, and prevent future occurrences that can be used in Colombia's coal mine closure framework.

detail.abstract: This note examines how unstratified (pooled) multiple-choice exams can conceal systemic weaknesses in student preparation. Using a FEBA-style 40-item final drawn from an unbalanced bank across four subject areas, we derive the expected scores and variances under stratified versus pooled designs. Stratification fixes content proportions, making weaknesses consistently visible, while pooling introduces “composition noise”: random variation in subject exposure that obscures structural deficiencies. Analytical results show that pooling increases score variance and, under skewed banks, depresses average performance. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that pooled designs yield grade downgrades relative to stratified exams, even when underlying abilities are identical. This design choice effectively converts a systemic educational problem into apparent random luck, raising concerns about fairness and psychometric validity. Recommendations include enforcing content blueprints, applying score weighting, or equating across forms to restore comparability.

title: Sovereign Loans Explained a Practical Guide to Global Lending and National Debt

detail.title: Sovereign Loans Explained a Practical Guide to Global Lending and National Debt
detail.abstract: Sovereign borrowing the act of nations taking loans is a central mechanism of modern economies. Loans finance infrastructure, stabilize currencies in crises, supply budget support, and sometimes serve strategic geopolitical aims. This paper explains, in clear and practical terms, how countries borrow, who lends to them, where lenders obtain funds, how loan contracts are structured, how repayments and restructurings work, and the risks that arise from these arrangements. Using extended case studies (Greece, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and the United States) and a set of comparative examples, this research maps common debt patterns and shows their relevance to entrepreneurs, investors, and informed citizens. The goal is to make sovereign debt transparent and actionable: to help readers understand how macro level borrowing affects markets, business decisions, and everyday financial life.

Regarding the topology of the interbank network, we confirm the high level of network stability but observe a higher density and a higher in– and out–degree symmetry than what is reported for unsecured markets.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the evolving role of the European Union (EU) in the South Caucasus, a region marked by geopolitical complexity and historical tensions. The primary aim is to explore how the EU can effectively engage with South Caucasian states to promote stability, economic development, and democratic governance. Central to this investigation are key research questions: What obstacles hinder effective EU engagement? How can regional cooperation models be structured to ensure mutual benefit among the states involved? What strategies can the EU adopt to enhance its role as a facilitator of peace in the region? Through a comprehensive analysis of existing literature and recent EU initiatives, the study identifies critical challenges such as external influences from neighboring powers and the diverse political contexts within the region. It highlights effective cooperation models that emphasize shared interests and collective benefits, suggesting that an EU-led framework could anchor regional collaboration while promoting aspirations for sovereignty among South Caucasian states. The findings indicate that for the EU to be perceived as a credible partner, it must adopt a more context-sensitive approach, integrating local realities into its strategic framework. Additionally, fostering economic interdependencies and promoting cultural exchange are essential for building trust and initiating dialogue. The overall conclusion posits that a transformative EU strategy can play a pivotal role in redefining the geopolitical landscape of the South Caucasus, transitioning it from a contested space to one characterized by pluralism, cooperation, and sustainable development. This study underscores the importance of collaborative frameworks that prioritize both regional ownership and external support, ultimately contributing to a peaceful and prosperous future for the South Caucasus.

detail.abstract: We present a workable outline of how ecosystems can be defined and used in the existing antitrust framework. We acknowledge that the concept of ecosystems comes up frequently in antitrust cases and policy documents, especially in digital markets, but also that, its recurrent invocation notwithstanding, competition authorities have not found ways to meaningfully integrate it into their work. This piece proposes practical ways ecosystems can be made useful in competition law enforcement and provides links to underlying research to further assist with the application of ecosystem analysis.

title: Inflation, Debt Overhang and Corporate Investment
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), University of Lethbridge - Dhillon School of Business, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Finance and William Paterson University

detail.title: Inflation, Debt Overhang and Corporate Investment
detail.abstract: We develop a model to examine the impact of inflation on corporate debt overhang and investment. Within this model, we characterize how inflation influences corporate investment decisions through two key mechanisms: sticky cash flows and fixed nominal debt coupons. Our findings reveal that expected inflation delays corporate investment through the discount rate channel, while reducing firms' cash flow stickiness could partially alleviate this delay effect. More importantly, expected inflation mitigates debt overhang by lowering the real burden of corporate debt, thereby encouraging firms to invest earlier. This phenomenon is more pronounced when corporate debt has a longer maturity. Finally, we test these predictions using a sample of U.S. firms and present new evidence that supports our theory.

title: Public Debt in the DRC
affiliations: Université Catholique de Bukavu

detail.title: Public Debt in the DRC
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the macroeconomic effects of public debt in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) by using a stochastic volatility SVAR model (SVAR-SV) 1. The main objective is to understand the dynamics of public debt and its interactions with the real economy, in a context characterized by a high vulnerability to exogenous shocks and persistent structural weaknesses. The results show that the volatility of economic growth is strongly influenced by internal and international shocks. Public debt, for its part, presents a contrasting dynamic: after a period of high instability until the mid-2000s, it experienced a relative stabilization from 2010, driven by management reforms and the support of external partners. However, impulse response functions reveal that a positive shock to public debt initially leads to a significant contraction in growth, suggesting a limited capacity to transform debt into productive investments. Furthermore, this shock induces a temporary decrease in public spending, an erosion of tax revenues, a depreciating pressure on the exchange rate, and an increased fiscal instability.

title: The Importance of the SSM’s Fitness and Propriety Work for Banks’ Performance – Evidence From 10 Years of SSM Work

detail.title: The Importance of the SSM’s Fitness and Propriety Work for Banks’ Performance – Evidence From 10 Years of SSM Work

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: In this paper, we empirically investigate how suitability concerns detected by the SSM in the fitness and propriety of management body appointees impact the performance of European banks in the period 2014-2023. We provide evidence that management body appointees where the assessment of the supervisory authorities raised concerns, had a negative impact on the bank’s future performance. The negative effect can be attributed to appointees where the supervisory assessment revealed such severe concerns that ancillary measures were imposed. These results outline the importance of the SSM’s work for safeguarding the quality of bank’s corporate governance and suggest that the Supervisors seem to be effective in pointing out those appointees that exhibit severe concerns. In addition, we find that the designation of female appointees by supervised entities increased the bank’s performance sustainably. This result indicates that stimulating diversity, in terms of gender, in the management bodies of banks positively contributed to bank performance.

title: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Banks and Non-banks in Times of Stress
affiliations: , European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Banks and Non-banks in Times of Stress

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effects of monetary policy on banks and non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), with particular attention to the role of financial stress. We use high-frequency identified monetary policy shocks and state-dependent local projections to capture non-linear responses across financial sectors. Drawing on aggregated balance sheet data, including total assets, debt securities, and loans, we find that monetary tightening leads to broad-based contractions in total assets and debt holdings, with particularly pronounced effects for banks and investment funds. Loan responses are more heterogeneous, but money market funds and pension funds exhibit notable declines in loan exposures, especially under high-stress conditions. Importantly, we find that financial stress significantly amplifies the contractionary effects of monetary policy across all sectors and asset classes. Our results highlight the differentiated roles and vulnerabilities of financial intermediaries in the transmission of monetary policy and underline the importance of financial conditions in determining its overall effectiveness.

title: Unions in Developing Countries

detail.title: Unions in Developing Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The effects of trade unions on firm performance are theoretically ambiguous. The sizable empirical literature on their effects is almost exclusively confined to developed countries, particularly those in North America and Europe. We contribute to the literature by estimating union effects on firm performance in about 40,000 firms in 77 developing countries between 2002 and 2011. In doing so, we exploit standardized firm level data collected by the World Bank. We find positive partial correlations between unionization and firm labor productivity and wages, especially in lower-income countries. These positive effects persist when we instrument for union presence, consistentwith recent evidence of union positive effects on productivity and wages in western industrialized countries.

title: The Effect of Broadband Internet on Mental Health-Related Disability Insurance Claims
affiliations: University of Konstanz and Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB) - Department of Applied Economics (DULBEA)

detail.title: The Effect of Broadband Internet on Mental Health-Related Disability Insurance Claims

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine the causal impact of high-speed internet on adult mental health using administrative data from Belgium. We exploit predetermined telecommunications infrastructure and broadband technology's distance-sensitive nature for identification. Our difference-in-differences estimates show internet increased mental health-related disability insurance claims by 0.054 percentage pointsa 31% increase relative to the control group. These findings are supported by increased antidepressant use at the municipality level. Results point to a work-related mechanism: effects are concentrated among knowledge workers and those in high work-from-home potential jobs. Time-use data show a substitution from leisure to work and less social interaction on weekends.

title: Errors in Survey and Administrative Data on Employment Earnings: Austria and the United Kingdom Compared

The model allows for measurement error in the administrative data and linkage error as well as survey measurement error. We find several cross-national similarities in error structure but also intriguing differences in error component probabilities, means, and dispersions.

title: Walking the Talk? Bank Climate Commitments and Green Lending in Emerging Markets
affiliations: University of London - Royal Holloway, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and University of London, Royal Holloway College - Department of Economics

detail.title: Walking the Talk? Bank Climate Commitments and Green Lending in Emerging Markets

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: We document how banks' voluntary climate commitments predict both their green lending practices and their borrowers' environmental investments. Using structured surveys of 644 bank CEOs and heads of credit across 33 low- and middle-income countries, we develop indices of banks' green management and lending practices. These unique organizational data reveal that banks signing international climate initiatives ('talk') indeed exhibit stronger green practices ('walk') than non-signatories. We then merge our bank data with detailed surveys of 4,719 firms and show that firms borrowing from climate-committed banks are more likely to undertake green investments. Exploiting geocoded bank branch and firm locations, we further find evidence of spatial matching: environmentally-oriented firms preferentially borrow from climate-committed banks in their vicinity. These patterns are consistent with voluntary climate commitments reflecting genuine environmental orientation rather than greenwashing.

title: The Shift from Persistent Inequality to Earnings Instability in Belgium
affiliations: , Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER) and University of Antwerp

detail.title: The Shift from Persistent Inequality to Earnings Instability in Belgium

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using rich administrative data from 2005 to 2021 for Belgium, this paper analyses how earningsdynamics differ across socio-demographic groups, focusing on gender and education. We find that while permanent earnings inequality remains the dominant source of overall earnings inequality in Belgium, it has declined modestly in recent years. We further decompose the sources of permanent inequality and find that this decline is mainly driven by reductions in between-group inequality, especially between men and women, and falling permanent earnings inequality among women. These factors combined, outweigh the disequalising effects from compositional shifts in the educational structure of the population. On the other hand, earnings instability has risen, particularly for the low- and medium-educated and more generally for men. These groups additionally exhibit higher persistence in transitory shocks. Our findings show that stability in overall inequality trends can mask structural changes in the nature of inequality, and highlights the importance of exploring the heterogeneity in earnings dynamics across skill groups.

title: Developing a New European Indicator of Potential Skill Shortages

detail.title: Developing a New European Indicator of Potential Skill Shortages

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Skill shortages are a type of skill mismatch whereby employers are unable to fill existing vacancies due to a lack of suitably qualified and/or skilled candidates. Despite representing a significant concern for policy makers, both at national and EU level, the literature on skill shortages is hugely underdeveloped. There is a lack of clarity and consistency on how skill shortages are defined and measured. In this study, using data from the 2021 European Skills and Jobs Survey combined with Lightcast job vacancy data, we attempt to bridge the methodological gap by developing a measure of potential skill shortages that can be readily replicated across countries over time. We estimate that approximately 2% of job vacancies in the European Union are likely to experience skill shortages. However, there is substantial variation across occupations, ranging from 5.1% for ICT professionals to approximately zero in more elementary occupations. There is also substantial variation in the estimated incidences of potential skill shortages at member state level. Our analysis also shows that occupations that are most likely to experience skill shortages also tend to experience relatively high rates of changes in skill requirements over time.

title: Beyond the Border: Labor Market Effects of U.S. Immigration Enforcement Policies in El Salvador

detail.abstract: By 2020, one in four Salvadorans lived abroad, with 88 percent residing in the United States. The remittances to GDP ratio was about 25 percent, highlighting the countrys dependence on migration. This paper examines the effects of a major U.S. immigration enforcement programSecure Communitieson migration and labor market outcomes in El Salvador. Using a shift-share identification strategy, we find that larger exposure to the program decreases the likelihood that a household includes a migrant, consistent with increased forced returns. These effects lead to lower income among male workers, particularly low-educated, informal workers, and those in agriculture. We also document a decline in the probability of receiving remittances. The findings suggest that a closure of migration opportunities can increase labor market competition and strain local economies. Effects are most pronounced in municipalities with limited absorptive capacity, underscoring the unintended consequences that U.S. immigration enforcement generates abroad.

title: Tariff Cuts, Policy Uncertainty, and the Force of Many: The Impact of Plurilateral Agreements

detail.title: Tariff Cuts, Policy Uncertainty, and the Force of Many: The Impact of Plurilateral Agreements

detail.abstract: Do countries gain more by liberalizing trade together than alone? To answer this question, we study the 2015 Phase II expansion of the Information Technology Agreement (ITA), which eliminated tariffs on products covering over 12% of world trade. Market access rose by 4–6%. Nearly half of this effect reflects coordination spillovers—the extra gains from simultaneous liberalization—outweighing the roles of direct tariff cuts and reduced policy uncertainty. Exploiting quasi-experimental variation in the number of countries liberalizing each product, we show spillovers are positive once coalitions span about two-thirds of world imports—below the commonly assumed 80% critical-mass benchmark for plurilaterals. These findings show that joint liberalization yields benefits beyond the sum of individual actions—evidence of the force of many.

title: Monetary Policy, Heterogeneous Expectations, and the Return of High Inflation
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Monetary Policy, Heterogeneous Expectations, and the Return of High Inflation

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies the transition to high inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic, using a behavioral version of the New Keynesian model, which replaces the conventional assumption of Rational Expectations with subjective and heterogeneous expectations. Different shares of agents in the economy form expectations based on alternative views regarding future economic variables: 1) a share of agents forecasts that inflation and output will rapidly revert to steady state; 2) another share forms forecasts based on a model resembling the MSV solution under rational expectations; 3) a third share of agents uses an under-specified model that captures trend-following, adaptive, or extrapolative behavior. Agents learn over time the parameters of their perceived model and they can also shift across different views based on past forecasting performance. The macroeconomic model is estimated using Bayesian methods to fit realized macroeconomic variables and data on expectations from surveys. The results document an additional channel that operates through switches in agents’ perceptions and amplifies the impact of the original inflationary shocks. In response to rising inflation after COVID, agents begin shifting from the mean reversion model to the trend-following specification (with a belief about perceived inflation persistence that is simultaneously revised upward). Consequently, the impact of inflationary shocks is magnified and the effects of monetary policy attenuated.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the Nobel Prize shapes the level and direction of innovation, drawing on a unique dataset of 466 Nobel laureates and 1,876 nominees in Physics, Chemistry, and Medicine throughout the 20th century. Leveraging the 50-year confidentiality rule on nominations, I implement a dynamic difference-in-differences design that compares innovation in winners'  fields with those of non-winning nominees. The analysis reveals a significant post-award increase in patenting within the patent classes of Nobel laureates, as well as spillovers into adjacent fields with a temporal lag. The surge in patenting is mirrored by an increase in publications whose titles and abstracts contain the same n-grams as prize-winning papers. These findings suggest that the Nobel Prize not only boosts innovation in the awarded topics but also fosters broader scientific exploration over time.

title: The Economics of Government

detail.title: The Economics of Government
detail.abstract: The inspiration for this textbook came from a famous quote by Thomas Jefferson, one of the founding fathers of the United States. He stated, “Whenever the people are well-informed, they can be trusted with their government.” For example, communism failed economically in Russia because the Soviet government controlled every aspect of its markets and economy. On the other hand, the communists control a flourishing China because the Chinese government embraced the ideas of free markets and unleashed the entrepreneurial spirit and drive of the Chinese people. Thus, the Soviet economy stagnated, while China continues to thrive and prosper. The political system itself is not important, but rather the relationship between the government and its society. We study this relationship comprehensively in this textbook. We dedicate each chapter to a specific aspect of government and its impact on the economy. Students can use this textbook as a first course in public economics or as a supplement to an introductory course in microeconomics or macroeconomics. Furthermore, readers can use this textbook as a reference guide for individuals seeking a comprehensive book on the economics of government without majoring in economics.

title: Beyond Firm Characteristics: Forecaster Heterogeneity Explains a Large Portion of Over and Underreaction *

detail.title: Beyond Firm Characteristics: Forecaster Heterogeneity Explains a Large Portion of Over and Underreaction *
detail.abstract: A vibrant literature in finance seeks to understand whether subjective expectations exhibit underreaction or overreaction. This literature has focused almost exclusively on characteristics of firms (in the field) or artificial assets (in the lab). We argue that the literature has neglected a substantial source of variation in over and underreaction: forecaster characteristics. Using IBES data, we show that forecaster heterogeneity explains roughly the same amount of variation in over and underreaction as firm heterogeneity. We obtain a similar result using existing laboratory data. Our results suggest that the search for drivers of over and underreaction needs to include forecaster characteristics.

title: How Climate Risk Shapes U.S. Systemic Stability through Syndicated Lending
affiliations: University of Venice - Department of Economics, ICMA Centre, Henley Business School, University of Reading and University of Reading - Henley Business School,

detail.title: How Climate Risk Shapes U.S. Systemic Stability through Syndicated Lending
detail.abstract: This study examines how climate risks influence systemic risk through the U.S. syndicated loan market. It combines eight established climate risk measures with a new proxy for banks' environmentally friendly orientation, along with sixteen region-specific indicators capturing short-term anomalies, long-term drought conditions, and extreme events. The analysis identifies four key drivers of systemic risk: banks' environmental stance, extreme events in the South, precipitation anomalies in the East, and shifts in U.S. climate policy. The findings indicate that while banks are exposed to risks arising from climate-sensitive regions, environmentally friendly lending contributes to greater stability. However, current climate policies are not effectively reducing uncertainty, and stronger policies are needed to promote sustainable lending and support financial stability, particularly in the Southern and Eastern regions.

detail.title: How Market Structure Shapes Entrepreneurship and Inequality
detail.abstract: The US economy has experienced a secular increase in markups, declining entrepreneurship rates and increasing income inequality since the 1980s. To reconcile with these secular trends, I propose a theory of entrepreneurial choice with strategic competition among heterogeneous agents. Agents' decision to become either an entrepreneur or a worker is directly shaped by their competitors. I quantify the model for the period between 1988 and 2018 and find that technological change in the form of both higher fixed costs and more dispersed technologies, as well as a less competitive market structure can explain these trends. Viewed through the lens of the model, the primary factor underlying these secular changes is the increasing dominance of highly productive entrepreneurs who inhibit the entry of other productive agents, resulting in fewer entrepreneurs, higher markups and rising income inequality.

title: ASMem: Anchor Sparse Memory for Multi-Domain Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models

detail.title: ASMem: Anchor Sparse Memory for Multi-Domain Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can become outdated or inconsistent over time, particularly when deployed across multiple knowledge domains. To address this, we study multi-domain knowledge editing, focusing on three core properties: reliability (accurate incorporation of new knowledge), generality (ability to correctly answer related queries), and locality (preservation of unrelated knowledge). Specifically, we empirically analyze two key issues: trade-offs among these properties and the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting during editing. Motivated by these insights, we propose Anchor Sparse Memory (ASMem), a plug-and-play editing module that isolates edits into parallel memory-specific parameters. ASMem introduces a novel anchor prototype routing mechanism to enable precise query-to-memory alignment and mitigate semantic interference during editing. Additionally, an efficient unsupervised clustering-based partitioning strategy assigns memory modules to distinct semantic domains, thereby guiding clear knowledge boundaries. Extensive experiments on real-world hallucination correction and Chinese linguistic editing tasks show that ASMem significantly outperforms previous methods, achieving higher reliability and generalization while maintaining locality over multi-domain long edit sequences. Further experiments validate the generality of our method. It can be readily extended to other families and scales of LLMs, demonstrating competitive performance.

title: Domestic Politics and Foreign Policy: The Case of Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
affiliations: O P Jindal Global University

detail.title: Domestic Politics and Foreign Policy: The Case of Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
detail.abstract: This article examines how domestic politics and foreign policy interacted in Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (2009-2025). It argues that Netanyahu fused ideological conservatism with pragmatic realism, focusing on national security while managing international pressures. Key examples include the Abraham Accords (2020), the judicial reform protests (2023), and the October 7 Hamas attack. These events show how security threats and diplomatic challenges bolstered Netanyahu's domestic standing, while foreign policy successes enhanced internal stability. The study highlights a feedback loop between internal unity and external assertiveness, suggesting that Netanyahu's leadership redefined Israel as a regional power, albeit at the cost of heightened polarization at home and abroad.

title: Does Mobility Make a Nice Person? Theory and Evidence from Across the Globe
affiliations: Jinan University - College of Economics

detail.title: Does Mobility Make a Nice Person? Theory and Evidence from Across the Globe
detail.abstract: It is easy to understand how cooperation might be achieved in small communities where members interact repeatedly, but in our modern world, there is a high degree of “relational mobility" where individuals often change locations and/or social groups, making repeated interactions difficult. How does this affect cooperative behaviors? I examine this question from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. I first apply the so-called voluntarily-separable repeated prisoner’s dilemma where players have some ability to leave the relationship. Greater voluntary mobility leads to more unconditional cooperation in equilibrium, and the model predicts a stronger effect when players are more patient. However, in terms of conditional cooperation, voluntary mobility also allows players to escape future punishment, thereby making its effect ambiguous. Involuntary mobility always weakens cooperation. I take these predictions to the data by first conducting a meta-analysis of twelve prisoner’s dilemma experiments that varied the amount of mobility in and out of relationships, and I find evidence that voluntary mobility increases cooperation but weakens reciprocity. I also examine the predictions of the model using data from the World Values Survey and Gallup World Poll, and the result is consistent with the theory on when and how the comparative statics appear.

detail.abstract: Using the example of the recent developments in the law relating to electronic trade documents (ETDs), this article examines the roles which international trade law plays in enabling digital trade through the application of the principle of functional equivalence in domestic laws and transnational regulation. It analyses the Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records (MLETR) and ETD legislation in the UK, US, and Singapore, and finds that functional equivalence can be applied in two waysthe unified and the dual-track systems-in providing an electronic alternative to the traditional paper transferable documents and instruments (transferable papers) used in global trade. Comparing the approaches employed by these common law jurisdictions in resolving the age-old common law 'possession problem' in relation to ETDs, the article recommends the most suitable template for legal reform on the subject in other common law countries.

detail.abstract: This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the Decentralized Monetary Exchange Market Index (DMI-FX), a composite index designed to measure the extent of currency trading shifts from traditional centralized markets to decentralized blockchain-based exchange platforms. With the increasing proliferation of decentralized financial systems, understanding the impact of this shift on foreign exchange market dynamics becomes crucial. This research reviews the key components of the DMI-FX index, including DEX Volume Share, Decentralized Liquidity Pool (DLP) Ratio, Crypto-Fiat Correlation Index, DEX Trading Pairs, and Stablecoin Adoption Index. The research also discusses the index calculation methodology and how it can be used as a powerful analytical tool to monitor structural changes in the foreign exchange market, identify opportunities and risks arising from decentralization, and assess currency risks associated with exposure to digital currencies. This work aims to provide valuable insights for policymakers, investors, and researchers to understand and adapt to the evolving landscape of the foreign exchange market in the decentralized era.

detail.title: Social Capital and Its Changes in Armenia: Challenges and Expectations
detail.abstract: Social capital was the Achilles" heel of the economic competitiveness of Armenia. In the meantime, the country made significant progress in solidifying it since the Velvet Revolution. In this article, we tried to present and analyze those elements of social capital which demonstrated significant progress in post-revolutionary Armenia, as well as the changes thereof. For that purpose, we have formulated the following research questions: What factors led to this growth, and what factors still lag? What hidden challenges can be observed through factual indicators which probably resulted from the slight decrease in the updated scores? What changes can be expected from the turbulent world and in the postwar society? The applied methodology is quantitative. In particular, to answer the research questions we used index analysis, graphic analysis, and comparison, correlation analysis techniques, pared t-test of the mathematical-statistical significance of changes, and Principal Component Analysis. The results of the analysis showed that a significant increase in the level of social capital was recorded in post-revolutionary Armenia, which was mainly due to the progress in institutional trust. Nevertheless, some revealed anomalies and encountered challenges undermined the archived progress in the growth of trust. Therefore, we put forward several recommendations.

title: Aircrafts and Application of Admiralty Jurisdiction in Nigeria

detail.title: Aircrafts and Application of Admiralty Jurisdiction in Nigeria
detail.abstract: When the old High Court of Admiralty in England was replaced under the terms of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act 1873 by a new Division of the High Court of Justice known as the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Court Division, the transformation was humorously referred to as the bundling together of 'wills, wives and wrecks.' This suggested a perception that the new Division's jurisdictional mandate was somewhat incongruous! This paper examines the intersection of admiralty jurisdiction and aircrafts within the context of Nigerian law, primarily the provisions of the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act 1991 (AJA) and the various admiralty procedural rules that have been enacted under the AJA's authority. On initial consideration, it may not appear far-fetched that admiralty jurisdiction has been extended to aircrafts given that both ships and aircrafts are ambulatory chattels and can traverse several locations including international boundaries. However, this paper argues that the application of admiralty jurisdiction to aircrafts in Nigeria now needs to be carefully circumscribed to avoid conflicts with obligations accepted under international treaties and to avoid overreach in the exercise of delegated legislative powers.

title: Limits to LTD, Loan Supply, and Real Effects: Banks vs. Nonbanks
affiliations: The University of Manchester - School of Social Sciences

detail.title: Limits to LTD, Loan Supply, and Real Effects: Banks vs. Nonbanks
detail.abstract: We study the transmission of macroprudential policy to loan issuance by banks and nonbank financial intermediaries, and the associated real effects on firm-level outcomes including mergers and acquisitions. We use loan-level data from the global syndicated credit market, information on the type of participating lenders between banks and nonbanks, and shocks to regulatory limits to the banks' ratio on loans-to-deposits (LTD) to document that a LTD policy tightening reduces credit supply by banks and simultaneously shifts financial intermediation to nonbanks. We show that this credit migration is driven by nonbanks that are less regulated and free from leading the loan arrangements. We also find evidence that in response to tighter LTD, borrowing firms with stronger nonbank relationships are shielded more by the decline in bank credit with ensuing relative increases in corporate assets, employment, and capital investment. Finally, firms in countries with better access to nonbank credit increase the number of acquisitions they undertake, although we do not identify a differential response when LTD policy changes.

title: Financing Africa's Infrastructure: The Imperative of Domestic Money Pools
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Financing Africa's Infrastructure: The Imperative of Domestic Money Pools
detail.abstract: Africa's infrastructure ambitions cannot be met without foreign capital. Yet external money alone cannot succeed. Its effectiveness depends on local controls that are grounded in trust. Domestic money pools-savings associations, chamas, pension funds, and sovereign wealth vehicles-provide these controls. They already mobilise trillions of dollars across the continent and embody the norms and values that bind African societies. This paper shows that money pools are more than repositories of cash. They are control structures: they discipline flows between state, market, and society; they capture real-time signals about confidence and risk; and they can direct long-term savings into infrastructure. The so-called formal capital market will only mature when pools are freed from the fiscal captivity of lending to the state. Foreign investors must adjust their attitude, recognising institutional trust as collateral. The African Development Bank is pivotal in brokering this alignment, ensuring global capital works through Africa's own institutions.

title: Sky Wars: Escalation Pathways in the Age of Solar Geoengineering
affiliations: University of Oxford and University of Leicester

detail.title: Sky Wars: Escalation Pathways in the Age of Solar Geoengineering
detail.abstract: As the salience of Solar Radiation Modification (SRM) - also known as Solar Geoengineering - rises, there have been increasing discussions of the possible security and conflict implications of these technologies. This piece looks at SRM through the lens of securitization and how SRM can securitize climate change and related disasters. Critically, SRM can enable climate disasters to be attributed to SRM-deploying actors. By creating a "threatening Other" on which to blame climate change, securitisation and exceptional measures, such as conflict, can be pursued in response to climatic events. Using past work, this piece builds a typology of conflict pathways and explores how the causal mechanisms illuminated by securitisation help explain conflict risk in these scenarios. Finally, with conflict-inducing-securitization in mind, we add a new, unexplored, conflict risk which outlines how conflict could occur in response to counter-geoengineering-a response to SRM which has been seen as an offramp for conflict risk.

title: Toward Computational Political Science: Artificial Intelligence as Methodological Enhancement for Institutional Analysis

detail.title: Toward Computational Political Science: Artificial Intelligence as Methodological Enhancement for Institutional Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper positions artificial intelligence and machine learning methods as evolutionary enhancements to established quantitative political science traditions rather than revolutionary replacements. Through comprehensive benchmarking against foundational work by Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, classical game theorists, and early computational pioneers, we demonstrate how AI addresses computational limitations that constrained earlier methodological innovations while maintaining theoretical rigor. Using standardized datasets including ACLED, V-Dem, UCDP, and Correlates of War, we establish performance benchmarks comparing AI ensemble methods against Expected Utility Models, examining prediction accuracy, temporal stability, and methodological scope conditions. Results indicate AI methods can achieve comparable or superior accuracy to Bueno de Mesquita's documented 90%+ success rates while extending analytical capabilities to multi-dimensional policy spaces and handling computational complexity that exceeded earlier technical capabilities. This work demonstrates AI's role as the natural next step in computational political science's evolution from Coleman's mathematical sociology through contemporary quantitative methods.

detail.abstract: This paper synthesizes evidence on three linked structural forces reshaping economic and civic life in the United States: (1) the acceleration of industrial automation—particularly in China—within globalized supply chains; (2) the widening skill mismatch in U.S. labor markets, where demand for technical trades and applied competencies remains high even as traditional degree pathways are uneven in their labormarket payoff; and (3) the persistence of mass incarceration and high recidivism rates that weaken human capital formation and intergenerational mobility. We argue that tariffs alone are an imprecise tool for reshoring and wage growth when production networks are highly automated and geographically flexible. Instead, a comprehensive strategy should center on workforce preparation (especially high-quality vocational and apprenticeship pathways), reentry and second-chance hiring, and local ecosystems that pair firms’ technology adoption with people-centered skill investment. We close with a 10-paper series plan to develop the agenda in detail.

detail.abstract: Although individuals are assumed to have many common motives in their utility functions (e.g., wealth/resources, safety/security) they nonetheless exhibit materially varying behaviors. This paper proposes a new model of utility maximization based on an individual's dynamic portfolio of "sub-utilities" each weighted as a function of the individual's genetic architecture, developmental history, evolutionary biases, and environmental feedback. Changes to utility over time are captured by a dynamic updating rule.

detail.abstract: Quantum computing promises computational capabilities unattainable by classical machines for specific problem classes. This paper lays out the physics that underpins those promises, distinguishes accurate claims from persistent misconceptions, and assesses credible impact pathways. We begin from first principles-superposition, entanglement, measurement, and interference-then explain why entanglement cannot transmit information on its own (the no-communication theorem). We survey hallmark protocols (teleportation, superdense coding) and algorithms (Shor, Grover, and selected linear-algebra primitives), and we confront the central engineering challengefault-tolerant error correction-emphasizing the surface code and recent experimental milestones. We outline the role of quantum networks (repeaters, entanglement distribution), clarify the relationship between quantum and classical channels, and conclude with societal implications: the cryptography transition is already underway at NIST, near-term quantum simulation prospects in chemistry and materials, and longerterm opportunities and limits in optimization and machine learning.
